The record states that no app worker is an employee now and that the platforms prevailed under the old test, so employee status is absent from every contract. Section 2 of the example names A-1 for this, but A-1 is about enforcement.

question.text: Is the mandated term absent from some contracts that would otherwise be made?

answer.rationale: Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-061 (illustrative figures), A-1: the Act is enforced: audits and private suits with double damages make treating workers as contractors without a valid agreement costly.

question.text: Will most bound providers comply with the mandate in practice?

answer.rationale: Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-061 (illustrative figures), A-29: fare shares are not cut in the first months (30 days' notice; scrutiny at launch). The other money term of the contract here is the fare share.

question.text: In the short run, are the other money terms of these contracts (wages, prices) fixed by pay scales, contracts or raise cycles?

answer.rationale: Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-061 (illustrative figures), A-28: section 9 does not fix the fare share, and companies can cut fare shares and bonuses after launch.

question.text: Over the medium run, can the wage (or price) of these contracts adjust downward, for instance through smaller raises?

answer.rationale: No row in WE-061's assumption table; my estimate from the text. For workers at the margin of choosing employee status the cover and the floor are worth less than the 11% contributions, the top-up and the flexibility the company takes back (sections 4 and 5 of the example); A-5 puts only 65% of low-fare workers on employee status. Close to the cut-off.

question.text: For the marginal contract, is the term worth less to the recipient than it costs the provider?

answer.rationale: No row in WE-061's assumption table; my estimate from the text. Workers can sign the contractor agreement, work on several platforms (45% do), or move trips to Selvane (A-14), so their alternatives are not clearly worse than the platforms'. The example signs no incidence row.

question.text: Over the medium to long run, are the recipients' alternatives to bound contracts clearly worse than the providers' alternatives?

answer.rationale: Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-061 (illustrative figures), A-11: buyers of shares expect the Act to survive the court challenge and repeal campaign, so the platforms' shares are valued on expected earnings.

question.text: Are the providers' businesses valued on expected earnings, so that a lower expected return lowers their sale value?

answer.rationale: Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-061 (illustrative figures), A-16: companies, drivers' groups and unions can organize at a cost below their stakes.

question.text: Can the bound providers organize to lobby over the mandate at a cost below their stake?

answer.rationale: Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-061 (illustrative figures), A-16: companies, drivers' groups and unions can organize at a cost below their stakes.

question.text: Can the recipients of the term organize to lobby to widen it at a cost below their stake?

answer.rationale: Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-061 (illustrative figures), A-3: some hours on a trip pay below 16 per hour (about a fifth). The floor here is the Act's own section 5 (K2), not an existing minimum wage, which does not reach app workers; the question is answered for that floor.

question.text: Does an existing price floor (a minimum wage) hold the wage of some recipients, so that it cannot fall?

answer.rationale: Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-061 (illustrative figures), A-31: the floor's surplus of employee hours is rationed by stricter criteria than the counterfactual's dispatch ranking (shift allocation, acceptance thresholds); dispatch already ranks drivers by rating and acceptance.

question.text: Can providers tell in advance which applicants will cost them more under the term?

answer.rationale: Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-061 (illustrative figures), A-4 (loosely): platforms pass part of their added cost into fares, which presupposes that the other platforms, all with well over 100 workers, face the same cost. Taxis and the small cooperatives are not bound.

answer.rationale: Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-061 (illustrative figures), A-10: taxis are a substitute for some app rides at fares fixed by the city. The small delivery services (A-15, 0.5) are the other unbound rivals.

answer.rationale: Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-061 (illustrative figures), A-8: some services can be reshaped to meet the three conditions at a cost below the Act's burden.

answer.rationale: Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-061 (illustrative figures), A-15: some delivery services can operate with fewer than 100 Lanvik workers.

source_sentences: An app-based worker is an employee of the network company unless the company proves that (a) the worker is free from its control and direction in performing the work, (b) the work is outside the usual course of its business, and (c) the worker is customarily engaged in an independently established trade.
Section 3 applies to natural persons who perform rides or deliveries through a network company with 100 or more app-based workers in Lanvik.
The Department of Labor enforces the Act by audit; workers have a private right of action for double damages; the penalty for misclassification is 5,000 per worker.
The Department's budget is raised by 4 million a year from the general fund.
An employee shall be paid at least the state minimum wage for all engaged time.
A network company may elect to offer its app-based workers in Lanvik a contractor agreement; an election applies to all its Lanvik workers.
A worker who signs one is not an employee for the purposes of sections 5 to 7 for the following twelve months, and may revoke it at each anniversary.
Employee status must be offered as the default, on a separate screen, and the choice must be freely made.

context: Today no app-based worker is an employee; the counterfactual law is contractor status under the old common-law test, under which the platforms prevailed in the courts, and the existing minimum wage, overtime and insurance laws do not reach them.
Platforms set and change workers' fare shares and bonuses unilaterally, usually several times a year, with 30 days' notice.
About 20% of hours on a trip pay less than 16 per hour on a trip (bicycle couriers on short orders, long low-fare rides).

readings: U1-a: no. A worker may log off at will, so only time on a trip, and any shift a company schedules, is engaged time
U1-b: yes. The apps reduce the priority of workers who decline requests, so all logged-in time is engaged time
unclear.text: Is time logged in and waiting time "during which the worker is required by the network company to remain available"?
